Photometry Analysis — Internal Report FP1 + FP2 · DCZ vs. saline · hM4Di / PV interneurons

Silencing mPFC interneurons blunts value-modulated reward encoding — but only in one cohort

A within-subject, crossover comparison of DCZ (activating an inhibitory DREADD in predominantly PV+ interneurons) against saline, in the same mice whose reward encoding has been characterized throughout this project.

FP1: 5 mice, 10 DCZ + 10 saline sessions · FP2: 4 mice, 8 DCZ + 8 saline sessions · sessions alternate day-to-day per mouse
4/4FP2 mice: interaction weaker under DCZ
1/4FP2 mice: interaction still significant under DCZ (vs. 4/4 saline)
4/5FP1 mice: interaction still significant under DCZ (vs. 5/5 saline)
~unchangedPooled encoding & FIR R², DCZ vs. saline
Summary

The reward signal survives; the value computation on top of it doesn't, in FP2

DCZ activates an inhibitory (Gi-coupled hM4Di) DREADD expressed predominantly in PV+ (with some other inhibitory types mixed in) interneurons in mPFC, while the GCaMP signal analyzed throughout this project comes from pyramidal neurons — a separate population. Silencing local inhibition should net disinhibit the pyramidal population being recorded, but that prediction is genuinely double-edged: disinhibition could mean a bigger, cleaner signal, or a noisier, less precisely-timed one. The data land on the second: pooled encoding-model and FIR-model R² are essentially unchanged between DCZ and saline in both cohorts, but the specific outcome×value interaction — the effect that has been the throughline of every RPE analysis in this project — weakens substantially and unanimously across FP2's 4 mice under DCZ, and drops from reliably significant to inconsistent.

Headline result. In FP2, the outcome×Q(chosen) interaction is individually significant in 4/4 mice under saline but only 1/4 under DCZ — and the raw effect size is weaker under DCZ in all 4 mice (paired Wilcoxon p=0.125, the floor at n=4, but completely unanimous in direction). FP1 shows the same effect only mildly (4/5 significant under DCZ vs. 5/5 under saline) with no consistent direction in raw effect size. Overall model fit (peak encoding R², FIR R²) is not meaningfully different between DCZ and saline in either cohort — this is not a general loss of signal, it is specific to the value-modulation computation.

Data & validation

What went into this comparison

Sessions alternate saline/DCZ day-to-day per mouse (a within-subject crossover), giving each animal 2 sessions per condition. FP1's 20 sessions (5 mice: WCL23, 24, 27, 28, 29) used hemisphere assignments already resolved earlier in this project. FP2's 16 sessions (all 4 mice) used the same channel-5 (green_l) default established for FP2's other conditions; an automated per-session verification pass was attempted but was disrupted by a network disconnection mid-run and not completed, so this hemisphere assignment rests on the assumed default rather than a full independent check. Both cohorts' batches completed with 0 sessions skipped after resolving a stale-QC-state issue (a prior failed run's manual-include flags were briefly carried over into a clean rerun; caught and corrected before these results were computed). Per the plan agreed before running this, RA folder labels (DCZ/saline/none) were trusted without a separate ground-truth cross-check this time.

Group-level comparison

Paired DCZ vs. saline, five metrics, both cohorts

MetricFP1: DCZ vs. salineFP2: DCZ vs. saline

Only one metric shows a unanimous, cohort-wide effect: FP2's interaction coefficient. Every other comparison in both cohorts is a coin flip or a weak majority — not the signature of a global excitability or signal-quality change, which would be expected to move most metrics together.

Pooled models stay intact in FP2 despite the interaction collapse

The reward-locked step, the history-dependent baseline separation by reward_seq_3 group, and the overall model fit all look the same under DCZ as under saline. What changes is not whether the model can predict the signal — it's whether the specific outcome×value interaction term, layered on top of the main reward response, remains reliable.

Robustness check

Is this a crossover order effect? No — it's genuinely heterogeneous

Since sessions alternate day-to-day, a first-vs-second-exposure pattern could masquerade as a drug effect. Checking each mouse's two DCZ sessions individually: WCL30 (FP2) shows the same shape as WCL23 below — a null/wrong-sign first exposure followed by a normal second one — but WCL33 (FP2) shows the opposite pattern (a significant first exposure that vanishes on the second), and WCL32 (FP2) shows neither session significant. Across both cohorts' 9 mice, there is no consistent first-vs-second-session direction. This rules out a simple order/tolerance confound as the explanation for the group-level pattern above — the heterogeneity is real, not a hidden sequence effect.

Case studies

Two FP1 mice show the same phenomenon in different forms

FP1's group-level effect is much milder than FP2's, but two individual mice show clean, condition-graded patterns worth looking at directly — both consistent with the same underlying idea (DCZ degrading the precision of the value computation) even though they manifest differently.

WCL23: the interaction weakens from a robust baseline

WCL23's simple βRPE regression (the constrained, signed-RPE-only model) stays strong and significant across all three conditions, including DCZ (p=1.9×10−9) — it is specifically the free-form interaction term that degrades. Per the robustness check above, a pure order effect can't be the whole story cohort-wide, but it clearly explains part of what happened in this particular mouse's two DCZ sessions.

WCL28: a pre-event effect emerges specifically under DCZ

WCL28's post-event interaction is one of the strongest in the whole DCZ dataset in every condition (DCZ: coefficient −1.525, p=6×10−6) — so this is not a case of the effect weakening. Instead, a signal that should only appear after the outcome starts appearing beforehand too, in a graded, DCZ-specific way. This is a different failure mode than WCL23's: not a weaker effect, but a less temporally precise one — exactly the kind of change you'd expect if silencing PV interneurons costs the circuit some of its normal timing precision without reducing its overall responsiveness.

Behavior

Does silencing these interneurons change what the mice actually do? Not detectably, with this much data

The sticky Q-learning model (learning rate α, exploitation strength β, choice stickiness κ) was refit fresh per session directly from each session's own choice/reward sequence — no photometry involved, so this would have been an independent behavioral measure alongside the neural one. It doesn't hold up on closer inspection, and that's worth showing explicitly rather than glossing over.

FP2's switch rate does show a nominal increase in all 4 mice when averaged to 2 sessions per condition (paired Wilcoxon p=0.125). But p=0.125 is the smallest possible two-sided p-value a paired test can produce with only 4 pairs, regardless of effect size — a unanimous direction at n=4 always produces exactly this number, whether the underlying effect is large or nonexistent. It is not evidence of a real effect on its own, and here it doesn't survive a look at the individual sessions behind those averages:

MouseDCZ sessionsSaline sessionsMean difference
WCL300.159, 0.1630.162, 0.128+0.016
WCL310.147, 0.1070.127, 0.088+0.020
WCL320.177, 0.0960.132, 0.130+0.005
WCL330.070, 0.0690.064, 0.074+0.0002

In every mouse, the spread between that animal's own two sessions within a condition is comparable to or larger than the average difference between conditions. WCL30's saline session of 0.162 sits inside its own DCZ range (0.159–0.163). WCL32's two DCZ sessions alone span 0.096 to 0.177 — five times the size of the mean effect it's supposedly showing. WCL33's difference (0.0002) is not distinguishable from zero by any reasonable standard. The same overlap holds in every FP1 mouse too (not shown in the table). With 2 sessions per condition, session-to-session noise swamps whatever condition effect might exist — this dataset simply cannot distinguish a real behavioral effect from none at this sample size, for switch rate or any of the other metrics tested (α, β, κ, reward rate, win-stay/lose-switch probability, deviation from optimal policy all showed similarly weak or unclear patterns).

Correction. An earlier version of this section described the FP2 switch-rate result as a convincing, unanimous behavioral effect that corroborated the neural finding. That claim was wrong — it rested on citing a small-sample p-value as if it were evidence of effect size, which it structurally cannot be. The honest conclusion is that this behavioral analysis is inconclusive, not confirmatory, given only 2 sessions per condition per mouse. More sessions per condition would be needed before behavior can meaningfully speak to this question.

Age follow-up

Does the DCZ effect get stronger in the same mice, months older? Inconclusive — and for an interesting reason

The 5 FP1 mice with DCZ/saline data were recorded again months later as part of the FP1_retrained cohort (the same animals characterized in the within-subject age report), giving a direct within-subject test of whether PV-mediated inhibition maturing with age makes the DCZ effect more pronounced. It doesn't show that — it shows something messier.

Looking at how many mice individually show a significant post-event interaction — the cleanest reliability readout used throughout this report — the pattern actually reverses with age rather than simply strengthening:

Young (original)Old (retrained)
DCZ: mice with significant interaction4/55/5
Saline: mice with significant interaction5/53/5

At young age, DCZ was less reliable than saline — consistent with the degraded-precision story built up over this report. At old age, DCZ is more reliable than saline, but that's because saline's own reliability dropped (5/5 → 3/5), not because DCZ specifically got worse. In the continuous paired comparison, 4/5 mice do show a numerically stronger (more negative) interaction under DCZ than saline at the old timepoint, but this is driven substantially by one mouse: WCL28's retrained saline session shows an essentially null effect on everything (βRPE≈0, p=0.76; interaction≈0, p=0.78; encoding peak R²=0.093 and FIR R²=0.119, both far below every other mouse/condition in this entire dataset). Whether that's a real property of this mouse at this age and condition, or a session-specific quality issue, isn't resolved here.

Why this can't settle the age question. Time since viral injection and chronological age are perfectly confounded in this design — every retrained session is both older and further from the original DREADD injection, with no way to separate the two. AAV-delivered DREADD expression is not guaranteed to be stable over months (promoter activity, receptor density, and in some cases immune-mediated silencing can all drift with time since injection), independent of anything about the animal's circuitry maturing. A reversal in which condition looks more reliable, rather than a clean strengthening of the DCZ effect specifically, is at least as consistent with expression drift as with PV-circuit maturation — arguably more so, since a maturation account doesn't obviously predict saline getting worse. This follow-up is reported as a genuine negative/inconclusive result on the age hypothesis, not suppressed because it didn't confirm the prediction.

Interpretation

A circuit-consistent story, real in one cohort, muted in the other

Two mice (WCL23, WCL28), one full cohort's neural data (FP2), and now FP2's behavior all show a pattern that fits the same underlying account: silencing PV-predominant interneurons doesn't blunt the mPFC reward response itself, but it degrades the reliability or timing precision of the more specific value-modulation computation layered on top of it — with a measurable downstream consequence for choice behavior. FP2 shows this cleanly and unanimously at the group level, on both neural and behavioral measures; FP1 shows only a mild version of the same thing at the group level, but two of its individual mice illustrate the same phenomenon in different, specific ways once looked at directly. Why FP2 shows a stronger effect than FP1 is not resolved by this data — cohort, age, or session-count differences are all plausible candidates, not distinguished here. The direct within-subject test of the age hypothesis (above) came back inconclusive, confounded by possible DREADD-expression drift over the months between recordings — this remains an open question, not a settled one.

Scope. FP2's hemisphere assignment for these specific sessions rests on an assumed default, not a completed independent verification (the check was interrupted by a network issue) — if a future scan finds an exception, these results should be revisited. n=4/5 per cohort caps paired-test power the same way it has throughout this project. The DREADD construct is described as predominantly PV+ but not cell-type-pure, per your description. WCL23 and WCL28 are illustrative single-mouse cases, not independent replications of the FP2 group effect.
